title: METHODOLOGICAL CONVERGENCE IN COGNITIVE MAPPING RESEARCH: INVESTIGATING CONFIGURATIONAL KNOWLEDGE
research_question: To explore the extent to which tests designed to measure aspects of configurational knowledge produced analogous results (convergent validity) and to examine the role of task demands (spatial and location cueing) upon these results.

participants.description: 279 first-year geography undergraduates (aged 18-29) resident in Swansea, Wales, for approximately one term (9-10 weeks). The initial study had 177 participants, and a second study collected data from a further 102 undergraduates for partially graphic exercises.
participants.recruitment: Participants volunteered as part of their first-year geography practical classes and received no reimbursement. They had access to Ordnance Survey maps and geographical details of the Swansea area.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Sketch map test 1 (sk1): Draw a map of Swansea including coastline and important features.
Sketch map test 2 (sk2): Draw a map of Swansea including places or landmarks.
Sketch map test 3 (sk3): Draw a map of Swansea and locate 25 listed places with a point.
Spatial cued response test 1 (scr1): Add other places and landmarks to a base map with two reference points (geography department A, bus station B).
Spatial cued response test 2 (scr2): Add 25 listed places and landmarks to a base map with two reference points (geography department A, bus station B).
Spatial cued response test 3 (scr3): Add other places and landmarks to a base map with two reference points (geography department A, bus station B) and the coastline.
Spatial cued response test 4 (scr4): Add 25 listed places and landmarks to a base map with two reference points (geography department A, bus station B) and the coastline.
Cloze procedure test 1 (cz1): Identify places removed from blanked-out boxes on a grid map.
Cloze procedure test 2 (cz2): Identify 15 listed places removed from blanked-out boxes on a grid map.
Metric Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) test: Complete a matrix of distances in miles between 15 listed places.
Nonmetric Multidimensional Scaling (NMDs) test: Underline the place furthest from two others in a series of triads.
Projective convergence (proj) test: Mark direction and distance from a first place to a second place, with compass radius representing a fixed distance.
Orientation specification (os) test: Identify the correctly oriented configuration out of possible options for a set of three places.

findings.antecedent: Location cueing (respondents choose places to locate) in spatial cued response tests (scr1, scr3) vs. Location cueing (respondents locate designated places) in spatial cued response tests (scr2, scr4) (Analysis framework 25)
findings.test_statistic: t=5.47 (scr1 vs scr2); t=7.76 (scr3 vs scr2); t=5.64 (scr1 vs scr4); t=7.72 (scr3 vs scr4)
findings.mechanism: Location cueing introduces large residuals when respondents are forced to locate unfamiliar places.
findings.quote: location cueing produces r² values significantly lower than when respondents can choose which places to locate

findings.antecedent: Spatial cueing (presence of a base map with two reference points) in open location cued tests (scr1 vs scr3) (Analysis framework 25)
findings.mechanism: Increased spatial cueing provides anchors to familiar locations and logical cues for others.
findings.quote: The significant difference between the two open tests is due to the amount of spatial cueing.

findings.antecedent: Spatial cueing (presence of a base map with two reference points) in cued location tests (scr2 vs scr4) (Analysis framework 25)
findings.mechanism: Location cueing masks the effect of spatial cueing by producing a selection of common residuals across tests.
findings.quote: spatial cueing alters the results of open location cued tests and not the cued location cued tests (scr2(fam<4) vs scr4(fam<4), t=−1.23, p= 0.23)

findings.antecedent: Familiarity filter (fam<4) applied to location cued tests (scr2 vs scr4)
findings.consequent: Effect of spatial cueing on bidimensional regression r² values
findings.mechanism: Familiarity is a significant variable in determining configurational knowledge, and removing unfamiliar data reveals that spatial cueing did not have an effect when familiar data were used alone.
findings.quote: once the anomalies have been removed on the location cued tests using analysis framework fam<4 there is a significant difference (scr2(fam<4) vs scr4(fam<4), t=−2.63, p=0.017)

findings.antecedent: Location cueing in spatial cued response tests
findings.mechanism: Location cueing leads to large residuals, causing r² values to drop by 30-40%.
findings.quote: r² values can drop by 30-40 per cent because of location cueing

findings.antecedent: Familiarity filter applied to spatial cued response tests
findings.consequent: Reduction in r² values due to location cueing
findings.mechanism: The familiarity filter reduces the effect of location cueing on r² values to 3-20%.
findings.quote: the use of a familiarity filter will reduce this effect to only 3-20 per cent.

findings.antecedent: Spatial cueing (coastline) in spatial cued response tests
findings.quote: The spatial cueing effect of a coastline raises r² values by 5-10 per cent.

findings.antecedent: Spatial cueing (minimal) in spatial cued response tests
findings.consequent: Dominance of absolute distortion over relative distortion
findings.quote: Where there is minimal spatial cueing, absolute distortion is dominant regardless of the effects of location cueing upon the spatial product.

findings.antecedent: Spatial cueing (detailed) in spatial cued response tests
findings.consequent: Dominance of relative distortion over absolute distortion
findings.mechanism: Detailed spatial cueing provides a base scale, removing absolute distortion from misjudging scale.
findings.quote: This is reversed for the tests with detailed spatial curing where relative distortion is dominant.

findings.quote: the projective convergence test produces an s-shaped curve where there are large numbers of middle values.

findings.antecedent: Configuration containing Mumbles Pier (orientation specification test)
findings.mechanism: The west end of Swansea Bay (Mumbles Pier) distorts students' cognition, acting as a topological frame of reference.
findings.quote: The only significance difference was between the place indexes of configurations containing Mumbles Pier and those configurations devoid of that place.

findings.antecedent: Configuration not containing Mumbles Pier (orientation specification test)
findings.mechanism: The east end of the bay seems relatively undistorted.
findings.quote: The east end of the bay, however, seems relatively undistorted as indicated by the high configuration accuracy score for configurations not containing Mumbles Pier.

findings.antecedent: Configuration rotated 90° (orientation specification test)
findings.mechanism: High residuals from 90° rotation lead to reduced accuracy.
findings.quote: This rotation was found on the low spatially cued, spatial cued response tests (1 and 2), and the objective convergence test. It is these high residuals which lead to a reduction in the configuration accuracy scores.

findings.antecedent: Alternative configuration looking very similar to correct one (orientation specification test)
findings.mechanism: Misrecognition due to similar configurations.
findings.quote: The large residuals that are not the result of the 90° rotation are the result of an alternative configuration which looked very similar to the correct configuration.

mechanisms: Task demands (spatial and location cueing) influence data collection and results.
Location cueing introduces large residuals when respondents are forced to locate unfamiliar places.
Spatial cueing provides anchors and logical cues, increasing accuracy.
Location cueing can mask the effect of spatial cueing.
Familiarity is a significant variable in determining configurational knowledge.
Detailed spatial cueing provides a base scale, removing absolute distortion from misjudging scale.
Misrecognition due to similar configurations or connected neighbors.
Uni-to-multidimensional tests are abstract and cognitively demanding, requiring conversion of configurational knowledge into distance/direction estimates.
Tests may measure different components of configurational knowledge or the same components with different degrees of success due to cognitive processing or selective use of knowledge.
moderators: Analysis frameworks (systematic: all 25 places, 15 places, 6 places; data-defined: guess, fam<2, fam<4)
Presence of specific landmarks (e.g., Mumbles Pier)
implementation_implications: To increase the integrity and validity of studies concerning cognitive map knowledge, research designs should adopt multiple, mutually supportive tests.
Researchers should be aware of the limitations of techniques used to measure cognitive map knowledge, especially regarding task demands.

limitations: Respondents were all geography students with skilled knowledge in cartography, potentially limiting generalizability.
The study area (Swansea) had a strong, misleading topography with the coastline acting as a major frame of reference, which might influence results.
The difficulty of subjectively assigning sketch maps to categories (e.g., Pocock's classification) highlights a criticism of sketch mapping.
Low sample sizes in some test groups (e.g., initial study for partially graphic tests) might affect validity, though a second study was conducted.
The time-consuming nature of some tests (e.g., uni-to-multidimensional) limited the number of locations that could be used.
The high p-value threshold (0.306) for significance in Spearman correlations (Table 6) is unusual and might inflate the number of 'significant' findings.
